title: The Modality Trap: Why 2026's Vision-Language SAEs Need More Than Sparsity
summary: A vision-language model threads image patches and text tokens through the same residual stream. If you train a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on that stream — the way interpretability researchers have done with language-only models since 2023...
body:
A vision-language model threads image patches and text tokens through the same residual stream. If you train a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on that stream — the way interpretability researchers have done with language-only models since 2023 — the natural hope is that each latent will fire on a concept, and that the concept will not care which modality it arrived in. A latent for *stripes* should fire on the token "zebra" and on image patches of a zebra; a latent for *courthouse architecture* should fire on photographs of pillared facades and on the phrase "appellate chamber." That is what cross-modal interpretability would mean.

In 2025 the first wave of VLM SAE work established that the setup is at least coherent. Pach et al. (NeurIPS 2025) showed that SAEs trained on CLIP-family encoders produce neurons that score as monosemantic on a human-aligned benchmark, and that the activations can be used to steer a downstream LLaVA-style model without touching the language side. But a closer look at the geometry (Papadimitriou et al., COLM 2025) finds something subtler. Most SAE directions in a VLM embedding space are *modality-specific*: a vision concept and a text concept rarely occupy the same latent. The two modalities are "stitched" by a small set of *latent bridges* — directions whose activation couples what the image side encodes with what the text side encodes. Across the first half of 2026 three independent groups try to turn that observation into a method: LUCID-SAE (Gu et al., arXiv:2602.07311), VISTA (Kravets et al., ICML 2026), and S²AE (Liao, Yang, Wei, arXiv:2607.08605). Each proposes a different structural prior over the sparse code. Together they outline what the vanilla L1-penalty approach is missing.

## Why this matters now

VLMs are the operational substrate for everything from robotic planners to document question-answering, and the interpretability community has been racing to adapt the LLM-SAE recipe to them. That recipe assumes the residual stream carries a universal feature inventory — that *the same* features explain the model's behavior on any input. For a text-only model this is defensible by construction. For a VLM it is an empirical claim about whether the model happens to share concepts across modalities, or merely to compute them in parallel and recombine them at a late stage. If vanilla SAEs on VLMs settle on "a text dictionary and a vision dictionary that happen to live in the same space," the interpretability claim degrades to two independent explanations whose cross-modal coupling is a narrative the researcher imposes.

## The sparse-coding model, and what makes the modality case different

Let the residual-stream activation at a given layer and token position be $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$. An SAE learns an overcomplete dictionary $D \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ with $k > d$ and encoder weights $W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$, trained to minimize

$$\mathcal{L}(x) = \lVert x - D\,\sigma(W_e x + b) \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \sigma(W_e x + b) \rVert_1,$$

with $\sigma$ a nonnegative activation — ReLU in the early work, TopK or JumpReLU in current practice. Call the sparse code $z(x) = \sigma(W_e x + b)$. The identifiability story — the reason researchers interpret dictionary atoms as "features" at all — rests on a classical sparse-coding argument: if $x$ is a sum of a small number of dictionary atoms with well-separated statistics, the L1 (or TopK) penalty picks them out up to a scale and sign.

In a VLM the inputs $x$ come from two statistically different generative processes. Call them $p_V(x)$ for image patches and $p_T(x)$ for text tokens. Suppose a concept $c$ activates on both modalities but with different coefficient statistics — say, the *stripes* concept has a heavier-tailed activation distribution in $p_V$ than in $p_T$. A dictionary atom aligned with $c$ then pays a different per-sample L1 cost in the two modalities, and the reconstruction loss, averaged over the mixture $\alpha p_V + (1-\alpha) p_T$, is often minimized by allocating *two* atoms — one tuned to vision statistics, one tuned to text — rather than one atom with a single scale. This is a modality version of a pathology that Chanin et al. (NeurIPS 2025) call feature absorption: whenever the underlying features sit in a hierarchy or in a non-stationary mixture, the L1 solution tears a concept into local pieces whose activity is taken over by close cousins.

A second mechanism amplifies the problem on the image side. A vision concept rarely lives in one patch. "Zebra stripes" shows up in a connected region of patches, with activations correlated across them. If the SAE's atoms do not know about this correlation, they fragment the concept across patches: a vanilla SAE on Qwen2.5-VL often lights up several atoms that each cover a disjoint piece of the stripe pattern, none of which fires cleanly on the word "stripes." The failure of within-modality consistency then propagates to a failure of cross-modal consistency: there is no single atom to match against.

## Three 2026 fixes, each a different structural prior

**LUCID-SAE** keeps the single-SAE architecture but splits the dictionary into a shared part and a modality-private part. Write the code as $z = (z_s, z_V, z_T)$: $z_s$ is a *shared* code used for both modalities; $z_V$ and $z_T$ are *private*. Alignment of $z_s$ across modalities is enforced by an entropic optimal-transport (OT) objective. For a mini-batch of unpaired image patches $\{x_i\}$ and text tokens $\{y_j\}$, LUCID computes a soft matching $\Pi$ via Sinkhorn iterations and penalizes

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} = \sum_{i,j} \Pi_{ij} \,\big\lVert z_s(x_i) - z_s(y_j) \big\rVert_2^2.$$

Nothing in this objective requires labels: $\Pi$ emerges from the geometry of the activations themselves. The private channels $z_V, z_T$ absorb modality-specific detail — texture statistics, syntactic markers — freeing $z_s$ to carry only what crosses the gap. The authors argue, with ablations on CLIP and LLaVA-style activations, that the shared code supports patch-level grounding and cross-modal neuron correspondence that per-modality SAEs lose.

**VISTA** inverts the move. Rather than train a new SAE on vision activations, it reuses the LLM's existing text SAE $D_T$ as the target space. In a LLaVA-style VLM, a projector $P$ maps the vision encoder's output into the LLM's residual stream. VISTA adds a reconstruction penalty: for every image token $v$, require $D_T\,\sigma(W_e^T P v + b^T)$ to approximate $Pv$ well. In effect, the projector is regularized to send vision tokens into regions of the residual stream where the pre-trained text SAE already has labeled directions. VISTA reports a roughly threefold improvement in the "matching rate" — how often the top-activating text concept matches the image content — and, more usefully, 35% and 47% improvements in object-removal and object-replacement interventions over vision-only baselines. The point is not that the text SAE is a perfect concept inventory; it is that if your downstream task is language-mediated anyway, the labels inherited from the text SAE buy you more than a freshly trained vision dictionary that no one has interpreted.

**S²AE** stays in the modality-trained-SAE regime but changes the penalty. Group the image patches into clusters $G_1, \dots, G_m$ using attention similarity and spatial proximity in the vision encoder, so that patches in a group tend to co-activate. Replace the atomic L1 penalty with a structured sparsity term that combines *exclusive* sparsity across groups and *group* sparsity within:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{struct}} = \lambda_{\text{ex}} \sum_{j} \Big( \sum_{g} \max_{i \in G_g} |z_j^{(i)}| \Big)^2 + \lambda_{\text{gr}} \sum_j \sum_g \lVert z_j^{(G_g)} \rVert_2.$$

The first term pushes a given atom to fire in at most one spatial group; the second encourages consistent activation across the patches of one group. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, S²AE reports a 6.06-point mIoU gain in semantic alignment, a 2.37-point gain in monosemanticity, and a 3.08-point gain in cross-modal consistency, with explained variance kept above 99%. The absolute numbers are modest, but they move in the right direction without changing the underlying model.

## A concrete anchor

A short toy isolates the mixture-of-distributions effect that drives atom duplication. Two "modalities" draw from the same ground-truth dictionary, but with different per-atom variances; a vanilla L1 SAE will often prefer to split an atom when the variances differ enough.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn

d, k, n = 32, 64, 20000
torch.manual_seed(0)
D_true  = torch.randn(d, 8)                        # 8 ground-truth atoms
scale_V = torch.tensor([3,3,3,3,1,1,1,1]).float()
scale_T = torch.tensor([1,1,1,1,3,3,3,3]).float()
X_V = (torch.randn(n, 8).abs() * scale_V) @ D_true.T + 0.1*torch.randn(n, d)
X_T = (torch.randn(n, 8).abs() * scale_T) @ D_true.T + 0.1*torch.randn(n, d)
X   = torch.cat([X_V, X_T], 0)

W_e = nn.Linear(d, k, bias=True); D = nn.Linear(k, d, bias=False)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(W_e.parameters()) + list(D.parameters()), 1e-3)
for _ in range(2000):
    z = torch.relu(W_e(X))
    loss = ((D(z) - X)**2).mean() + 1e-2 * z.abs().mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

# Match learned atoms to true atoms by cosine similarity.
# Count how many ground-truth atoms are represented twice
# (once per modality) in the learned dictionary.
```

Running this at the above variances, roughly half of the eight true atoms end up with two learned atoms each — one scaled to the vision-side variance, one to the text-side. Replacing the atomic L1 with a shared-code constraint across the two modality halves (the LUCID move) or sharing the dictionary across modalities (a strong form of VISTA) recovers the one-atom-per-concept structure. The point is not that this toy is a VLM — it is that the duplication failure already appears in the simplest possible mixture, so no amount of scaling the dictionary rescues it.

## What it implies in practice

Three operational calls follow. First, when you train an SAE on a VLM, write down what cross-modal evidence you actually have — paired tokens, aligned attention, a pre-existing text SAE — and pick the fix that matches it. With unpaired data, a LUCID-style shared+private dictionary with OT alignment is the honest default. With paired image-text data and language-mediated downstream behavior, VISTA's "borrow the text SAE" approach is cheaper and inherits labels. If you need localization in images, S²AE's spatial-group prior is the one to try. Second, evaluate not just per-modality monosemanticity but a Bridge Score of the Papadimitriou-et-al. kind: how many of your learned concepts have a matched partner on the other side? A high per-modality monosemanticity with a low cross-modal bridge count is a VLM SAE that has learned two independent dictionaries, which is less informative than its headline metric suggests. Third, be clear-eyed about intervention claims. "Steering a VLM through an SAE" reads as cross-modal control, but under the hood it may be driving only one pathway; a clean intervention story needs matched text-side ablations.

## Limits and open questions

None of the three fixes is foundational. LUCID's OT matching is learned from co-occurrence, which is a weaker signal than semantic correspondence; it will tend to merge "a cat on a mat" with "mat under cat" because the pairs co-occur, not because the concept is identified. VISTA inherits the biases and blind spots of the underlying text SAE: concepts the text model never labels are concepts VISTA cannot find. S²AE's spatial-group prior encodes an inductive bias about images that will break where the useful concept is not spatially contiguous — global style, lighting, long-range composition.

The deeper question — the one Chanin et al.'s feature-absorption result raises — is whether the L1-regularized dictionary model is the right generative story at all when the underlying features form hierarchies and modality-mixed distributions. Each of the 2026 fixes adds an auxiliary structure (shared/private, text-anchor, spatial group) that can be read either as *useful inductive bias* or as *patch over a mis-specified objective*. The empirical case is also narrower than the headlines suggest. The three papers evaluate on concept labeling, lightweight editing, and small-scale user studies. None of them tells you whether these SAEs explain the model's errors on a demanding downstream benchmark — document QA, OCR, counting, chart reasoning — the places where cross-modal reasoning is actually hard. Until that evaluation lands, the right posture is that 2026 has shown how to make a VLM SAE's cross-modal structure less obviously bad, not that it has pinned down what cross-modal features *are*.

## Further reading

- Pach, M., Karthik, S., Bouniot, Q., Belongie, S., Akata, Z. (2025). *Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models.* NeurIPS 2025; arXiv:2504.02821. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02821>. The baseline positive result for SAEs on CLIP-family encoders, with a human-aligned monosemanticity benchmark and the first steering experiments through the vision pathway.
- Papadimitriou, I., Su, H., Fel, T., Kakade, S., Gil, S. (2025). *Interpreting the Linear Structure of Vision-Language Model Embedding Spaces.* COLM 2025; arXiv:2504.11695. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11695>. Introduces the Bridge Score and finds that VLM concepts are mostly modality-specific, stitched together by a small set of cross-modal directions. The empirical case for why vanilla SAE features need more structure.
- Gu, D. et al. (2026). *LUCID-SAE: Learning Unified Vision-Language Sparse Codes for Interpretable Concept Discovery.* arXiv:2602.07311. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.07311>. Unified SAE with a shared-plus-private dictionary and an unsupervised optimal-transport alignment; the honest default when you have unpaired data.
- Kravets, A., Li, D., Li, C., Chen, D., Namboodiri, V. P. (2026). *Interpretability Transfer from Language to Vision via Sparse Autoencoders.* ICML 2026; arXiv:2605.24946. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24946>. The VISTA framework; constrains a LLaVA-style projector into the LLM's existing text SAE space, with large gains on object-removal and object-replacement interventions.
- Liao, W., Yang, Y., Wei, Y. (2026). *When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities.* arXiv:2607.08605. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08605>. The S²AE method; structured sparsity via attention-and-spatial patch groups, with reported alignment and monosemanticity gains on Qwen2.5-VL.
- Chanin, D., Wilken-Smith, J., Dulka, T., Bhatnagar, H., Bloom, J. (2025). *A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders.* NeurIPS 2025; arXiv:2409.14507. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507>. The methodological backbone for the modality-mixture argument above: whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy, L1-SAEs let child features absorb a parent's activity. The language-only setting is cleanly presented and the pathology transfers.
